(p-189) Surah 'Amma Yatasa'alun, also called An-Naba'

Its central purpose is to demonstrate that the Day of Resurrection, whose occurrence they were unanimously denying, and about which they came to dispute with the believers after the Prophet ﷺ was sent, is established with a firmness that admits of no doubt or disagreement in any way. This is because the Creator of creation, who is wise and capable of whatever He wills, has arranged their affairs in the best arrangement: He built for them a dwelling and perfected it, and made them in such a way that their kind persists through themselves, so that they do not need any external thing that they could see. This was more conducive to their mutual affection and greater for the intimacy of some of them with others. He made their ceiling and their bedding serve their benefits. The Wise does not leave His servants, while He is in complete power and full authority, to revel, some oppressing others, eating of His bounty and worshipping other than Him, without accountability. How much more so when He is a judge, and how much more so when He is the Most Judicious of judges. This is something that is not permissible in reason and does not occur to the mind at all. Therefore knowledge of the Resurrection is certain. Each of its two names is clear in this regard, upon reflection on its verses, its beginning, its mention, and its end.

(Bismillah) the Wise, the All-Knowing, who possesses all the attributes of perfection. (Ar-Rahman) who equalized His servants in the basic apparent blessings: existence, rank and wealth, and in showing the straightest path by the guiding intellect, by revelation and by sending messengers. (Ar-Rahim) who singled out whom He wills for the completion of those blessings, so He granted them success in good deeds. Because He informed in Al-Mursalat of their denial of the Day of Decision, and judged that for them, on account of that, there is a doubled and repeated woe, and He concluded it by saying that if they disbelieve in this Qur'an, they will not believe in anything after it. He opened this surah by stating that what they disagreed about and denied the Messenger concerning his command does not admit of dispute, due to the clarity of the Qur'an's exposition regarding the wisdom of the Most Merciful, about which no two people differ, together with its inimitability in eloquence. So He said, marveling at them to the utmost degree, rebuking them, denouncing them, threatening them, and magnifying the matter, in the form of a question, drawing attention to the fact that one should not conceive of their disagreement, nor recognize the locus of their dispute. Therefore everyone should ask about it, even one who knows it, to inform that what they dispute, due to its clarity, is not believed to be disputed by any sensible person who opposes its command, and that questioning should not be directed except at what is obscure. So He said:

* *

﴿'Amma﴾ meaning "about what?" It was lightened in pronunciation and in its form by assimilation, and its alif was dropped because of its frequent recurrence and as an indication that this question is something that should be omitted. If it were not so, it would be concealed and the one who mentions it would feel shy, and it is made light. ﴿Yatasa'alun﴾ meaning the people of Makkah ask each other, and anyone who asks about something of the Qur'an, asking in doubt, hesitating and wavering, among themselves and between them and the Messenger ﷺ and the believers (may Allah be pleased with them). Because of the intensity of their amazement, their disputing, denying and obstinacy, when His verses are recited to them and His clear proofs are made manifest, is called simply "asking."

When He had magnified that about which they were asking, marvelling at them for it, He specified it with His words, to make known that this vagueness was only for the sake of magnifying it: ﴿about the great news﴾, that is, about the message of the Messenger, his bringing the Clear Book, his report concerning the Day of Decision, and the One who witnesses everything of that, Allah, through the inimitability of this discourse and through His firm and swift promise. And since it was in the position of glorifying it, He described it, for emphasis, with His words ﴿the great﴾, even though a nabaʾ (report) is only said of a great news [whose matter is weighty]. So in all of that there is an alert that it is incumbent upon every hearer to submit to it and to attend to its matter, not to doubt it or make it a subject of dispute. And He magnified their rebuke with His words:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 3:

﴿Concerning which they differ﴾, that is, with their inner convictions, although they claim that these are the most upright of convictions. ﴿They differ about it﴾ means they differ greatly and steadfastly. Some of them affirmed it and some denied it. Among those who denied it, some doubted and some were certain. Some said, "He is a poet," and some said, "He is a sorcerer," and so on [among the falsehoods]. That matter, which is the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), whose chief concern is resurrection after death, became highly confused for them, and they repeatedly questioned and interrogated one another about it, despite its greatness and the greatness of its manifestation. Something great should not be subject to disagreement (p-192) in any way. A person of dignity should not enter into any matter except with insight. How much more so when it is great, how much more so when its greatness is extreme, and how much more so when it is the most important matter that concerns him. It is therefore incumbent upon him to investigate it to the utmost, to seek its proofs, to examine its evidences, and to clarify its arguments, until, after knowledge of certainty, his matter reaches the certainty of sight, from the time he reaches adulthood until he dies. How much more so when the proofs are recited to them, decisive arguments are made clear to them, and clear evidences are brought to them, yet they remain obstinate, dispute, oppose, and evade.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: As for the surah of al-Naba' in its entirety, it is arranged around a question and an interrogation that arose from them. It seems to come here in the context of a turning away and a shift. As for His saying, ﴿No! They will soon know﴾ [An-Naba': 4] and ﴿Again, no! They will soon know﴾ [An-Naba': 5], it corresponds to the repeated threat in His saying, "Woe that day to the deniers." It is as if it had been said: they will soon know the outcome of their denial. Then God, exalted is He, presented some of His beautiful workmanship which, if the one who reflects considers it, he knows that nothing of it was created in vain. Rather, one learns a lesson from it and clarifies the wisdom behind it. Thus he knows that there must be a time when the veil is lifted, and when God requites creatures according to their states of reflection, contemplation, and humility before the One who established the totality (p-193) of those signs. He perceives, from the repetition of seasons, the renewal of conditions, and the revival of the earth after its death, that the same course applies to resurrection and the consistency of the judgment. To this refers His saying, ﴿Thus shall We bring forth the dead﴾ [Al-A'raf: 57]. God, exalted is He, also said, alerting to what we have mentioned: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting place?﴾ [An-Naba': 6], up to His saying, ﴿and gardens of thick foliage﴾ [An-Naba': 16]. These are the created things intended for reflection, as he previously stated. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is an appointed time﴾ [An-Naba': 17], that is, an appointed term for your recompense. If you had reflected upon what was mentioned to you, you would have known from it that it will occur, and that it will happen so that your recompense may come according to what preceded from you. ﴿So woe that day to the deniers﴾ [At-Tur: 11]. What supports this intention from the verses that follow is His saying, exalted is He, concerning what He prepared for the tyrants: ﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning﴾ [An-Naba': 27], ﴿and they denied Our signs with complete denial﴾ [An-Naba': 28], ﴿and We have enumerated everything in a record﴾ [An-Naba': 29]. Then He said afterward: ﴿Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success﴾ [An-Naba': 31], ﴿gardens and grapevines﴾ [An-Naba': 32]. And His saying afterward: ﴿That is the true day﴾ [An-Naba': 39]. As for the worldly life, it is play and amusement, and indeed the Hereafter is the true life. And His saying afterward: ﴿The Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forth, and the disbeliever will say, "Would that I were dust!"﴾ [An-Naba': 40]. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 4:

When the matter [of the Great Tidings] was of such magnitude, he said, emphasizing, because what they disputed about and asked concerning is not a place for dispute and questioning, [he used] the particle of deterrence, and so, threatening them and affirming their warning, he said: ﴿Nay!﴾ That is: what they asked about and disputed is not at all a matter open to dispute, and doubt can never reach it in any way. So let them desist from that and be restrained before (p-194) there befalls them that which they will have no power to withstand.

When it was as if it had been said: "Will what they are engaged in come to an end?", he answered with his words, threatening and omitting the object of the knowledge in order to magnify it, so that the soul goes off in every direction: ﴿They will come to know!﴾ That is: they will reach a point where their state, in abandoning obstinacy, will be the state of one who knows everything that benefits and harms them. This will be soon, by a promise that admits no breaking. Then, for them, will be the "eye of certainty" which cannot be resisted, after the "knowledge of certainty" which they had repudiated. The rank of this deterrence, threat, restraint and warning is magnified by his words:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 5:

﴿Then no!﴾ That is, the fact that His command is manifest in its appearance is a deterrent against disputing about His command. ﴿They will come to know﴾, that is, after death, after having known beforehand what will be of His command, by a true promise about which there is no doubt. Their state at that time will become the state of one who has been brought to submit, as they will be, between the humbled and the abased, the insignificant and the exalted. As for those whom We have chosen from among them for faith, they will be humbled [in obedience]; and those whom We intend to be wretched through disbelief, you will see them bowed down and abased. All will share in the experience of certainty [in its true sense]. This was indeed what the Mighty One said would happen after a short time, when the days of Allah overtook them, humbled their noses, and abased their foreheads. The reading of Ibn 'Amir, as it is reported from him, is with the second-person ta' (of address) in the threat, and it is more suggestive of entreaty toward the one who repents.

(p-195) When He had established their matter with the certainty of one who is utterly confident in what he says, He indicated this by something that admits of no doubt or hesitation at all. So He said, confirming for them and rebuking them for their questioning [by what He urged them to ponder and by the wondrous signs of His sight and the marvelous creatures which He originated from non-existence], a complete and great proof of the perfection of power together with the perfection of wisdom, which necessitates certainty regarding everything the Messengers alerted to concerning the laws, the Resurrection, and the Recompense, beginning with what is most intimately connected to them, namely the environment: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿a resting-place﴾, meaning a bed for you, a tractable place of settlement upon which one can remain steady, so that you may act upon it as you wish.

ﷻ "And the mountains as pegs?" That is: you know their strength and their greatness, and your inability with regard to even the least of their affairs, ﴿as pegs﴾ that hold them fast, just as a tent is not held up except by its pegs. The poet al-Afwah al-Awdi says:

"The tent is not raised except with its pillars,
and no pillar stands if the pegs are not driven in."

This is so that the earth does not sway with you. For it is suspended over the expanse of knowledge, held by the hand of power. Were it not for the mountains, because of their great weight, the earth would be like a high, empty ship upon the surface of the sea, in constant motion, especially when the wind is strong. At such times no one standing can keep his footing, no one sitting or sleeping can remain still. The mountains are thus like the heavy cargo that you lower into the water so that the vessel is steadied against excessive rocking. How, then, could it be sound in any way to hesitate in accepting the report of one whose power is this, especially when that which he has informed about is something whose matter He, glory be to Him, has fixed in the original natural disposition (fitrah), and whose truth He has established in the intellects with the clearest and most manifest establishment? (p-196)

When He had reminded them of what is in the container, which is their bedding, as an indication of the completeness of His power, He followed it with a reminder of what is in the contained, which is themselves, so that the signs of the self (anfus) and of the horizons (afaq) might come together, and it would become clear to them that He is the Truth. So He said: ﴿And We created you﴾, that is, with what indicates this from the manifestations of greatness, ﴿in pairs﴾: tall and short, handsome and ugly, male and female, for all your kinds, despite the distance of their regions and the remoteness of their dwellings, so that your species might endure until the time when your extinction occurs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 9:

When he had mentioned that which is the cause of the continuation of the species, he mentioned that which is the cause of its preservation from the swift onset of corruption, so he said: ﴿And We made﴾, that is, by the greatness We possess, ﴿your sleep﴾, which We constituted the body to be receptive of, ﴿a cessation﴾ [that is,] a cutting off from sensation and movement, which had wearied you during your day, along with its extension and continuance, as a relief for the animal powers and the bodily senses and a removal of their exhaustion. Although it is a cutting off from the perfection of life, it reminds one of the Great Death, while waking reminds one of the resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: al-subat (the cessation) is that one is cut off from movement while the spirit is still in him.

(p-197)

When he mentioned sleep, He followed it with its most fitting time, reminding of the blessing of the temporal container after reminding of the spatial container. So He said, indicating by the manifestation of majesty His greatness: ﴿And We made the night﴾, that is, after the departure of light, until it is as if it had never been, ﴿a garment﴾, that is, a covering and a veil that conceals by its darkness whatever falls upon it from the eyes, as clothing conceals the body, ﴿so that you may rest therein from livelihood-seeking﴾.

﴿And We made the day﴾, i.e., the one whose sign is the sun, ﴿a time of livelihood﴾, i.e., a time for movement, which is among the means of earning, which is among the means of livelihood (*ma'āsh*). Livelihood is *al-'aysh*, its time, and its place, making manifest what the night had concealed. So the verse is of *ihtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which two opposites are mentioned together, each one's counterpart being left implicit): it mentions clothing first as an indication of the omission of its opposite second, and livelihood second as an indication of the omission of its opposite first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 12:

When he had mentioned the cradle (mihad) and what is in it, he followed it with the ceiling, by whose revolving there come to be time and the age and what it contains of brilliant lamps and manifest benefits for the enlivening of the cradle and of the servants who dwell in it. So he said: ﴿And We have built﴾, that is, a mighty building, ﴿above you﴾, that is, encompassing every direction of above, and this is an expression that indicates encompassing; ﴿seven﴾, that is, of heavens; ﴿strong﴾, that is, they are at the utmost of strength and firmness, with no cleft in them and no rift; the passing of ages does not affect them, nor the passing of eons, until the command of Allah comes to manifest the great things that have been decreed.

When he had mentioned the roof, he mentioned some of what is in it of the foremost benefits, and so He said, indicating by the manifestation of greatness the greatness of it: ﴿And We have made﴾, that is, of what none other than We can do, (p-198) ﴿a lamp﴾, that is, a very brilliant star, ﴿blazing﴾, that is, it is, along with its radiance and the intensity of its light, hot and fiercely kindled, and it is the sun, from their saying: "al-jawhar wahaja" (the gem shone), and "al-jamr wahaja" (the ember blazed).

Ibn al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 14:

When He mentioned what destroys moisture by its heat, He followed it with what extinguishes heat by its moisture and coolness, whence arise food and drink, by which the life is completed. Their generation comes from the vessel (al-zarf) with the cradle (al-mihad) and the ceiling (al-saqf). He made this most like what is generated between the two spouses of offspring: the sky is like the husband, the earth is like the wife, the water is like the seed (al-mani), and the plants from the star and the trees are like the children. So He said: ﴿And We send down﴾, that is, from what others cannot do, ﴿from the squeezing clouds﴾ (al-mu'sirat), that is, the clouds which have become heavy with water, so that they approach the point where the winds will squeeze them and they will rain, just as the crop is harvested when its time to be harvested has come. Al-Farra' said: "al-mu'sir is the cloud that is adorned with rain but does not yet rain, like the woman who is mu'sira, namely the one whose menstruation has approached but who has not yet menstruated." [And] al-Razi said: "The clouds that are about to rain are like the mu'sira who is near to menstruation." ﴿abundant water﴾, that is, poured forth in abundance, one part following another. It is said: thajjahu, and thajja bi-nafsihi.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 15:

When he mentioned its beginning, he followed it with its end, saying: ﴿That We may bring forth﴾, i.e., by Our greatness, to which We have tied causes to their effects through means, ﴿thereby﴾, i.e., by the water [causing it through means], ﴿grain﴾, i.e., a plant bearing a kernel (ḥabb), which is its intended purpose, because the servants feed on it. He stated it explicitly because it is the intended thing, and he began with it because it is the sustenance by which life endures, like wheat, barley and others. ﴿And vegetation﴾, by which they take delight and enjoy themselves, and which cattle graze upon.

Since it is one of the observable matters that cannot be denied that the earth contains gardens beyond counting, he expressed it with the plural of paucity (jam' al-qillah) to belittle it in comparison with the dazzling greatness and the far-reaching command. So He said: ﴿And gardens﴾, meaning orchards that gather together kinds of trees and plants, the food-producing and others, ﴿luxuriant﴾, meaning with trees densely intertwined, gathered one against another because of the intensity of irrigation. It is the plural of laff, like jidh' (trunk). Al-Baghawi said: It has also been said that it is the plural of the plural: one says jannah lifa', its plural is luff, with a damma on the lam, and the plural of the plural is alfaf. What he mentioned included flowing and standing springs of water, so he sufficed with mentioning it over mentioning them. Muqatil said: Each of these things that He mentioned is more wondrous than the resurrection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 17:

When He had mentioned what indicates the utmost of power and the ultimate of wisdom, which definitively points to *al-wahdaniyya* (the oneness of God), for if there were plurality, wisdom would not exist and power would not be complete, this produced love for the one who possesses these attributes. Thus there resulted in the obedient person the longing for His meeting and the eagerness to behold the perfection of His blessings. And for the disobedient person there resulted what is fitting for him of fear of meeting Him, so that this might turn him back from his aversion and refusal. I say: I know that He mentioned it only to indicate the great news of the meeting with the Mighty, the Merciful. So He said, deriving a conclusion from what preceded of threat and what indicated the completeness of power, emphasizing it because of their denial: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision﴾ [i.e. -] which is the great news. Its warning has already been given in *al-Mursalat*, and He did not create the creation except to gather them in it and to manifest the attributes of perfection, so that He may decide in it between every confuser with a decision free of any doubt, and the oppressed may be taken back from the oppressor. ﴿Was﴾, i.e. in the knowledge and wisdom of God, an existence that is unavoidable, placed in it as an inherent nature is in beings possessing souls, ﴿a fixed term﴾, i.e. a limit by which the world is timed and at which it ends, along with the creatures in it.

When he had mentioned it, he mentioned what is in it, magnifying it and urging obedience to it. He said, ﴿The Day﴾ (*yawm*), functioning as a *badal* (substitute, apposition) of it or as a *bayan* (clarification) of it. Since what is terrifying and alarming is the blowing itself, not that it comes from a specific blower, he put the verb in the passive, saying ﴿is blown﴾ (*yunfakhu*), meaning: by a blower whom Allah has permitted ﴿into the Trumpet﴾ (*al-sur*), which is a horn of light, according to what has been said, whose breadth is greater than the distance between the heavens and the earth. This is the blast of resurrection, and it is the second of the blasts, as mentioned at the end of Surat al-Zumar. For this reason He said ﴿and you will come﴾ (*fa-ta'tuna*), meaning, after rising from the graves to the place of standing, alive, ﴿as you were the first time﴾, without losing any of your limbs, skins, hair, nails, or original colours, nor anything that would gather you from the earth after you had been scattered in it, and after the dust of those of you who decayed had mixed with its dust, and the dust of some of you with the dust of others. Distinguishing that, gathering it, and reassembling it as it was, and returning the spirit to it, is easy for Him, glorified and exalted be He, just as He did all of that from a drop of semen after He had done it to Adam, peace be upon him, from dust that had no basis in life. The state of your coming is ﴿in multitudes﴾ (*afwajan*), meaning nations, groups, and companies, walking and hastening, each nation with its leader.

Al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him. Our shaykh Ibn Hajar, in the biography of Muhammad ibn Zuhayr in *Lisan al-Mizan* (said: it is apparently fabricated), narrated that Mu'adh, may Allah be pleased with him, asked about these multitudes, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My nation will be gathered in ten categories: some in the forms of monkeys, some in the forms of pigs, some will be upside down, dragged on their faces; some will be blind, some deaf and dumb, some will chew their tongues, which hang down upon their chests while pus flows from their mouths, and the people of the gathering find them repulsive; some will have their hands and feet cut off; some will be crucified on trunks of fire; some will have a stench worse than carrion; some will wear robes of tar [full-length], clinging to their skins. They are: the tale-bearers, those who consume unlawful gain, those who devour usury, those who are unjust in judgment, those who are self-admiring of their deeds, scholars whose words contradict their actions, those who harm their neighbours, those who carry tales to rulers about people, those who follow their desires and withhold the right of Allah, the Exalted, and those who are arrogant out of vanity."

Having mentioned the sign within themselves, he (Allah) then mentioned some of the signs of the horizons, and began with the upper realm because it is more noble. So he said, using the passive form because the one who opens is absolute in opening (التفتيح), and because that is more indicative of the power of the Agent and of the ease of matters for Him: ﴿And the sky will be opened﴾. That is, this kind was split apart with great splitting. The Kufans read it with the light form (takhfif), because intensity (al-takthir) is indicated by what is consequent upon the opening, namely His saying: ﴿so it becomes﴾, that is, [all of it] becomes an existence as if it were its very nature, ﴿gates﴾, that is, very many, because of the abundance of the great rifts, to the extent that it became as if it had no reality except being gates.

When He mentioned the ceiling, He mentioned the earth's nearest and hardest parts to it, and so, again in the manner of the speech of those who have power, He said: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion﴾, that is, carried off with the least effort toward movement, ﴿the mountains﴾, despite what you know of their firmness and hardness in the air, as if they were scattered dust, and His saying ﴿and they will become﴾, that is, a firmly established state, ﴿a mirage﴾, that is, we see in them nothing but an illusion that appears while they are moving, passing by like clouds, and then they vanish because their parts are scattered like dust. How great is this majesty, before which hearts tremble and great distresses are magnified!

(p-203) When he had made clear that the Day of Judgement (yawm al-fasl, the Day of Decision) is the Great News, after having indicated it and mentioned what happens in it of the moving (of the mountains), he mentioned the final destination to the two abodes, so he said, after reminding of what the mountains contain of punishment through their roughness, and what is in them of wild beasts, insects, thorny trees, tangled cuts, and other wonders of divine decree, emphasising their denial: ﴿Indeed, Hell﴾, that is, the Fire into which its inhabitants are thrown, frowning at them with the utmost of what they dislike, ﴿has been﴾, that is, by its very nature and disposition, ﴿a place of ambush﴾, that is, a place of lying in wait for the enemies of Allah, where the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for them, and when they see them they drive them headlong into it; and for the friends of Allah, where the guardians of Paradise lie in wait for them to rescue them from the Fire when they arrive at it. Or it is a place of intense watching for the disbelievers, until it has become embodied as watching, because its inhabitants are gathered together, so that not one of them escapes, like al-mit'an (one who stabs much) for one who stabs often, and al-mikthar (one who multiplies) for one who exaggerates in multiplying. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that on the Bridge of Hell there are seven stations. At the first of them he is questioned about the testimony that there is no god but Allah. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the second, where he is questioned about the prayer. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the third (p-204) where he is questioned about the zakat. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the fourth, where he is questioned about the fasting. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the fifth, where he is questioned about the hajj. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the sixth, where he is questioned about the 'umrah. If he brings it complete, he passes on to the seventh, where he is questioned about the wrongs (al-maza'im). If he is cleared of them, well; otherwise it is said: Look, if he has any voluntary acts with which to complete his deeds. When he is finished, he is taken to Paradise.

For the transgressors, a place of return (ma'ab), that is, those who exceed the bounds of God. Since fear-inducing warning takes precedence over attracting benefits, He mentioned the warning first, saying: "For the transgressors" (lil-taghin), meaning those who go beyond the limits of God, "a place of return" (ma'aban), meaning a destination and an abode, after God had created them (dhara'ahum) for it, so that it was as though they had been in it. Then He prepared them, by their original natural disposition (fitrah), to come out of it and to distance themselves from it. Then, by means of the Scriptures God sent down and the messengers He dispatched, it was as though He had brought them out of it. Then they returned to it through the denial they had introduced.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 23:

When He mentioned their destination therein, He mentioned their remaining in it, so He said, as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "al-ṭāghīn" (the transgressors): ﴿Lābithīna fīhā﴾ (remaining therein). Since the plural of paucity (jamʿ al-qillah) is used metaphorically for the plural of abundance (jamʿ al-kathrah), and since al-ḥuqb (an age, a long period) is applied to an indefinite span of time, and is also applied to a specific limited period, it is said to be eighty years, and seventy thousand years. The context from the opening of the surah with "al-naba'" (the great news) and its description, together with the expression "al-naba' al-ʿaẓīm" (the great news), and what follows, indicates that the intended meaning is perpetuity if what is meant is that which has no limit, and that the intended meaning, if what is meant is the limited, is the plural of abundance. Most of what has been explained concerning al-ḥuqb is that it is for hyperbole, not for specifying a limit. So the plural of paucity here is not problematic. Whoever takes it to mean less than that, and it suffices him as a deterrent, the expression does not harm him. Whoever dares against it and makes light of it, it becomes a trial for him, just as restricting the number of the guardians of the Fire to nineteen did not harm anyone except himself. Therefore He expressed the period of remaining with His saying: ﴿Aḥqāban﴾ (ages), that is, great, consecutive eras without end. Moreover, the expression with it, even if it were taken to mean a lesser span and considered finite, does not contradict what was explicitly stated concerning eternity, because it affirmed one thing and did not negate what is beyond it. It is related from al-Ḥasan that he said: "al-ḥuqb is hardly mentioned except where the succession and continuity of times without cessation is intended."

Since a dwelling cannot be fit for habitation except with moderate conditions and water, which is the life of everything, He said, mentioning the state of this lingering: ﴿They will not taste therein﴾, that is, even for an hour, so how much less what is beyond tasting, ﴿therein﴾, that is, in the Fire specifically. It seems that by placing it first He indicated that they will taste in another abode the zamharir (the bitter cold), ﴿coolness﴾, that is, refreshment and rest, for its benefit to them from the heat, or cold in general, ﴿nor any drink﴾ of water or other that would suffice them against thirst (p-206) in any state whatsoever.

﴿Except﴾ that this drink is ﴿boiling water﴾, meaning water that is hot and scalds the faces, its heat having reached its peak; "and" that this drink, along with its heat, or its cold, is ﴿ghassāq﴾, meaning the essence of the people of the Fire, made of pus and blood, cold and foul-smelling. According to this reading, the exception is distributed: the ḥamīm (boiling water) belongs to the drink, and the ghassāq (intensely cold, foul discharge) belongs to the cold. Thus their drink in the realm of the Blaze (al-saʿīr) is ḥamīm, and the ghassāq belongs to the realm of the zamharīr (extreme cold).

When He had passed this judgment upon them, this punishment [which cannot be borne, He mentioned its wisdom], He said that He recompensed them with this, ﴿a fitting recompense﴾, meaning one that corresponds to their deeds, because they used to take people's wealth, and they would burn their chests over it, cool their drinks with it, describe it, and perfume it. So now they are burned by the foul extract of others, and it is as if, after the ages (ahqab) — if they are taken to be finite — they will be given a punishment other than the boiling water (hamim) and the dark, pus-like liquid (ghassaq).

Then He gave the reason for their punishment in His saying, emphasizing it as an alert that reckoning is so manifest that everyone affirms it, so it is hardly believable that anyone would deny it and not regard it as possible. So He said: ﴿Indeed, they used to﴾, that is, with what is for them like an innate disposition that accepts nothing other than that, so they corrupt the cognitive faculties, in that they ﴿do not expect﴾, that is, in any state whatsoever, even if they saw every sign, ﴿a reckoning﴾. So they do not act except for their desires. (p-207) This corresponds with their abiding forever in the Fire. He expressed their denial by the negation of hope because it is more eloquent, and that is because a person hopes for good with the slightest possibility.

When his hope of them was shown to be absent, which indicated their denial that corrupts the cognitive faculty (al-quwwah al-'ilmiyyah), he stated it explicitly in a more general manner, saying: ﴿And they denied Our signs﴾, that is, in light of the greatness they possess, which indicates that they come from Us, ﴿with complete denial﴾, that is, a denial that is at the utmost degree of exaggeration, to the extent that even if they heard the most false of falsehoods they would not deny it as they denied these [signs]. Thus their being made to drink what no one can properly drink, and even if one sips a little of it, one dies instantly without death, is a recompense for them for their denial of the scorching [signs] by which they make the truthful ones drink all kinds of burning. It was also recited with the lightened form (bi-l-takhfif), to indicate that they were lying in their denial.

Since the implied sense was: "So We made for everything a measure," he joined to it His saying: ﴿And everything﴾, meaning absolutely, of their deeds and otherwise, or everything upon which reckoning falls, ﴿We have enumerated﴾ (p-208). Since enumeration matches writing in precision, He emphasized its act with it, saying: ﴿in a Book﴾. So it is not permissible that We leave anything of things without recompense. The verse can be taken as ihtibak (a rhetorical device of mutual implication), which is the better reading: the verb of enumeration indicates the omission of its verbal noun and the affirmation of the verbal noun of "kataba" (to write) alongside it, i.e., "We enumerated it with enumeration and wrote it as a writing," and that enumeration and writing are for the absence of injustice.

When He mentioned His punishment and indicated its correspondence with their recompense, He made the saying directed at them, whether by the tongue of circumstance or by the tongue of speech, a consequence of their denial, as humiliation and an increase in the requital, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which signals the intensity of disgrace and anger upon them and the perfection of His power, glorified and exalted is He. So He said: It is permissible that it be a consequence of an implied element after "kitaban" (a book), such as: that He may recompense them for everything from Him, saying to them, through the tongue of the angels or the tongue of circumstance: ﴿So taste﴾, that is, of this punishment, in this state, because of your denial of the Reckoning. He emphasized their tasting in the future tense, so He said: ﴿So We shall not increase you﴾, that is, in anything whatsoever at any time ﴿except in punishment﴾. For your abode contains nothing but the Blazing Fire, just as the Garden contains nothing but bliss. Thus it is understood from this that the attainment of anything for them other than punishment is impossible.

(p-209) When He had mentioned the recompense of the disbelievers and had signaled at its end that it is a humiliation, He mentioned the recompense of the believers, who oppose them, saying, resuming (the discourse) and emphasizing it to refute the disbelievers' denial of it: ﴿Indeed, for the God-fearing﴾ — that is, those firmly rooted in fear, which necessitates taking precaution against what one fears, so they guarded themselves from the wrath of God by means of what pleases Him of deeds, words, and states — ﴿is a fulfillment﴾ [that is, a success] — and a place of success and a time of success, with lasting rest, from all that has been mentioned for the tyrants, who are their opposites, and who have fully exposed themselves to punishment. Then he explained it, or substituted for it (ibdal) by omitting a modifier, meaning "a place of success" (fawz):

Gardens (ḥadāʾiq), that is, orchards containing various kinds of trees bearing fruit, and fragrant plants, so that they combine the delight of taste with the delight of sight and smell. Walls surrounded them and enclosed them. Ibn Jarir said: "If there were no walls enclosing them, it would not be called a ḥadīqa (garden)." He singled out grapevines for their goodness, excellence and nobility, and for the delight of taste they contain. He referred to the trees by their fruit, to inform that they are found only laden with produce, and that their fruit is the greatest part of their benefit. So He said: ﴿and grapevines﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 33:

When he (Allah) mentioned the dwellings, which are pleasant, graceful and delightful, he mentioned what is enjoyed in them, which comprises the delighting of the senses: sight, touch and taste. So He said: ﴿And maidens of equal age﴾, meaning women whose breasts have become firm (kawā'ib, sing. kā'ib), ﴿of equal age﴾, meaning of one age, born of the same time as one another, having touched the dust at the same time as one another, not before the other. Rather, even if they were born, their birth would be at one and the same moment.

(p-210) When He mentioned the women, He mentioned what is suited to their companionship, saying: ﴿And a cup﴾ [i.e. of drink] from among the wines, for which there is no equal in the pleasure of taste, outwardly and inwardly, in perfection of delight, and in the reviving of the powers.

Since the custom has been that good drink is scarce, He indicated its abundance, as evidence of its excellence, by His saying: ﴿full﴾, i.e. brimming.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 35:

Since the gatherings of wine in this world are filled with what spoils them of idle talk and lying, except for those who have no sense of decency, for whom no ugliness spoils anything, He said, negating of it what would disturb the pleasure of hearing: ﴿They will not hear therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise, at any time, ﴿any idle talk﴾, i.e., any nonsense (laghat) deserving to be disregarded, because it is more general than being meaningless in the sense of having no meaning at all, or being used in a way that has no meaning existing in external reality, however slight, or having a meaning but one that does not produce any significant benefit. And since lying was negated in this manner, and since contradiction is a harm to the one contradicted, He negated it by His saying: ﴿nor any lying﴾ (kidhdhaban). This form is used both for mutual denial (al-takdhib) and for lying in general (mutlaq al-kadhib), so the meaning becomes: no harm through contradiction in speech. This agrees with the reading of al-Kisa'i with the light (takhfif) pronunciation, whose meaning is "lying" or "mutual lying." The majority reading uses the intensive (tashdid) form for the smoothness of the wording and its balance with "a'nabаan wa atraaban" (vineyards and maidens of equal age), while still hitting the meaning precisely, without any deviation from the intent and without any strain in any way.

(p-211) Since giving that is in exchange (mu'awadah) is more pleasing to the soul of the recipient, He said: ﴿a recompense﴾, and He made clear that He made it a recompense for them only as an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ). For He, glorified be He, is under no obligation to anyone, because no one can fully render the thanks due for a single blessing of His blessings, since even their deeds are among His blessings. So He said: ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to you by honouring your community with various kinds of honour. And in ﴿a gift﴾ there is an indication of this, for it is giving without return. ﴿Sufficient﴾, that is, in measure of sufficiency, even if a person among them does whatever he does; and it reckons all kinds of reckoning. From the expression of the Arabs, "He gave him, so he ahsaba him" (aḥsabahu), meaning when he followed up the giving upon him and increased it, until it exceeded counting, and he said: "Enough for me" (ḥasbī); it is not possible that he would be in need along with this gift, even if he increased his spending. The expression with it was chosen instead of "adequate" (kāfiyan), for example, because it has a greater effect on the soul, for it is said: if this is the reckoning, then what is the assumption regarding the reward?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 78, verse 37:

When Glorified is He mentioned the vastness of His grace, He described His Most Holy Self with that which indicates His greatness, as an increase in the honor of the one addressed, ﷺ, because the greatness of the servant is in proportion to the greatness of the master. So He said, in substitution according to the recitation of the majority, and in a break with the nominative on the basis of praise according to the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning their Originator, their Governor, and their Owner, ﴿and whatever is between them﴾, in dominion and possession. When that (p-212) included the Throne and what is below it, He gave the reason for it with His saying: ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, meaning the One to whom belongs the general bounty, the least of which is bringing into existence, and this belongs to no one other than Him, for all is included in His dominion and possession. Therefore, indicating His majesty after the attribute of mercy, He said: ﴿They have no power﴾, meaning the people of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, at all, in a lasting manner, at any time, in this world or in the Hereafter, not even on a specific day, ﴿to address Him﴾, meaning to the One of general bounty, specifically, ﴿[in] speech﴾, meaning that they address Him or address another with a word or more in their affair, in extreme concern for Him, by what the expression "address" conveys. How then with less than that? And if they do not possess that from Him, then from whom (could they possess it), when all belongs to His dominion and possession? That they do not possess the power to address them is an implication by agreement (mafhum muwafaqa). The summary is that they cannot address anything from their own selves, as is the case of an owner. As for others, they may be able to compel him to address them, or to address him without his permission and without his consent, and without his possessing it for them, since he has no possession. If this is so regarding address, then what is your opinion of one who claims union with Him through unification (ittihad) — may they be cursed, and theirs is the evil return. How bold they are in regard to unification! Al-Ustadh Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri said: How can there be for the created, originated being and the poor, miserable one any capacity by which he owns address from Him, or breathes a breath? Far from it! Rather He is God, the One, the Subduer.

(p-213) Since this might lead one to think that intercession is shut off in His presence, and since speech arises from the spirit, and since the angels are the closest of beings to spirituality, He emphasized this meaning, removing whatever might create that misconception about intercession. Whether or not we say that "the Spirit" here is a genus, He said, mentioning the time-frame of ﴿They will not speak﴾ ﴿on the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks﴾, meaning this genus, or a creation of God's creation of very great rank. It has been said that it is the angel appointed over the spirits, or Jibril (peace be upon him), or the Qur'an, referred to by such statements as ﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit by His command﴾ [al-Nahl: 2] and ﴿Thus We have revealed to you a Spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. This was said by Ibn Zayd. ﴿And the angels﴾, that is, all of them. By mentioning the lining up in rows, He drew attention to the severity of the matter, saying ﴿in ranks﴾, because of the terrible calamities of that Day and to guard the two weighty ones (the jinn and humankind), while they are in the middle of the circle of their rows, surging and agitated because of the magnitude of what they are in. Then He increased the matter's magnitude by mentioning the governing element of "on the Day," saying ﴿They will not speak﴾, meaning that from the moment all of them together come forth, not one of them will utter any word of speech at all, whether addressed to Him or to anyone else, whether it concerns a great matter or not, [not - ] any of them. It is possible that this describes the elite among them, so that the pronoun refers to them, and then others are included a fortiori. ﴿Except one whom the Most Merciful permits﴾, that is, to speak, by a special permission, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾, that is, the King whose blessings upon any of His creatures come only from Him, ﴿and who says what is right﴾. If the matter does not occur, then if no one at all speaks, this serves as a proof for the verse of address (ayat al-khitab, the verse concerning direct address), in that if the Spirit and those close to him are in this station, then in the state of everyone present, one would be most in need of speech. So what is the assumption about others? They are in the same condition a fortiori, and others are included in this and in other matters a fortiori. As for in this world, although no one speaks except by His permission, one may still speak in error.

When this day was magnified by the silence, out of awe of the Possessor of Majesty, ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108], He pointed to it with what it deserves, increasing its greatness, saying: ﴿That﴾, meaning the one pointed to, because of the remoteness of His station, the greatness of His rank, and the loftiness of His position, ﴿is the Day of Truth﴾, meaning in its being a Day, because it is established in itself, so it must occur and has no cessation, established without doubt for any intelligent person, and established in everything He affirmed, and false [every thing that] He negated. When He had established from His greatness what no other could establish the like of, and since He had created the faculties (quwa), the capacity (qadar), and the act through choice (ikhtiyar), it was incumbent upon every intelligent person to take up the means by which he is delivered. On this basis, as an alert to deliverance from it and an exhortation to it, He said: ﴿So whoever wills﴾, meaning the taking, from among the responsible persons to whom He has granted permission, ﴿takes﴾, meaning with the utmost of his effort, ﴿a way to his Lord﴾, meaning to his Creator, the Benefactor to him, or the Lord of that Day, by using the faculties which Allah gave him in righteous deeds, ﴿a return﴾, meaning a place of return, which is the return in which he obtains reward through faith and obedience. For Allah has given them power and choice, but none of them can will anything except by the will of Allah. (p-215)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 78, verse 40:

When, in this surah, he had presented from the explanation of this momentous tidings the wisdoms, admonitions, subtleties, promise and threat that he had presented, he summarised it in his saying, emphasising it against their denial: ﴿Indeed, We﴾, by reason of the majesty that is Ours, ﴿have warned you﴾, that is, O nation, and especially the Arabs, through what has passed in this surah and other than it, ﴿of a punishment﴾. Since its coming was unavoidable, and its occurrence was the same whether it was by death or by resurrection, and since everything whose coming is certain is near, He said: ﴿near﴾.

When He had warned against it, He specified its time, intensifying it to magnify its terror, [so He said]: ﴿the Day when a man will look﴾, that is, a man of its kind, the righteous among them and the wicked, looking with doubt concerning it, ﴿at what﴾, that is, that which ﴿his hands have sent forward﴾, that is, what he earned in the world of good and evil. He expressed by the two hands, because they are the seat of power, so he used them as a metonymy for it, although most of what one does is done by them, either independently or jointly, whether good or evil.

Since the implied sense was: "Then the believer will say: 'Oh, I wish I had stood up before this!'", He conjoined to it His saying: ﴿and the disbeliever will say﴾, that is, the one deeply immersed in disbelief, when he sees, from [those - ] terrors, wishing for the impossible: ﴿Oh, I wish I had been﴾, that is, a state of being that is necessary and does not cease, ﴿dust﴾, that is, in the world, so that I had not been created and had not been held to account, or in this Day, so that I would not be punished. What is meant by him is the species, or Iblis, who was arrogant toward prostrating to Adam, peace be upon him, who was created from dust, and magnified himself with praise and boasting by being created from fire. He says this when he sees what Allah has prepared for Adam, peace be upon him, and for the special ones of his descendants, of honour and everlasting bliss, and for this arrogant one against his Creator, of the perpetual punishment that does not cease. It is related from Abu Hurayrah and Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah, exalted is He, will exact retribution on the Day of Resurrection for the beasts from one another, then He will say to them: "Be dust," and they will become dust, and the disbeliever will wish for the like of that. So it is known that this Day is of utmost greatness and that it must occur. Hence, questioning about it for the sake of wonder at its occurrence is among the greatest ignorance. Thus its last part returned to its first, and its joints bent most fittingly to what connects them, and it linked with what follows it most fittingly. For the one at the point of death, struggling with the pangs, sees many of the terrors, convulsions and fears, for the sake of which he wishes that he had been cut off from the world, having no connection with it on any day of the days or any night of the nights. And Allah is the Granter of success to what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final resort.
